Isovolumetric relaxation, rapid filling, reduced filling, atrial systole and rapid ejection

questions.sec: The 0.8-Second Cycle, the 0.3-Second Systolic and 0.5-Second Diastolic Phase Lists, the 70 to 30 Per Cent Filling Split, and the S1 Valve Apparatus with Annular Contraction and Coaptation

questions.sec: The 0.8-Second Cycle, the 0.3-Second Systolic and 0.5-Second Diastolic Phase Lists, the 70 to 30 Per Cent Filling Split, and the S1 Valve Apparatus with Annular Contraction and Coaptation

opts: AV valves are open with 70% passive filling, atrial systole adds 30%, then atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure and the AV valves close, producing S1
AV valves are open with 70% passive filling, atrial systole adds 30%, then ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure and the semilunar valves close, producing S1
AV valves are open with 70% passive filling, atrial systole adds 30%, then ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure and the AV valves close, producing S1
AV valves are closed with 70% passive filling, atrial systole adds 30%, then ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure and the AV valves open, producing S1

questions.sec: The 0.8-Second Cycle, the 0.3-Second Systolic and 0.5-Second Diastolic Phase Lists, the 70 to 30 Per Cent Filling Split, and the S1 Valve Apparatus with Annular Contraction and Coaptation

questions.sec: The 0.8-Second Cycle, the 0.3-Second Systolic and 0.5-Second Diastolic Phase Lists, the 70 to 30 Per Cent Filling Split, and the S1 Valve Apparatus with Annular Contraction and Coaptation

Annular dilatation → leaflets separate (coaptation zone) → sudden tensing of the leaflet → S1
Papillary contraction → chordae shorten → leaflets evert → S1

questions.sec: The 0.8-Second Cycle, the 0.3-Second Systolic and 0.5-Second Diastolic Phase Lists, the 70 to 30 Per Cent Filling Split, and the S1 Valve Apparatus with Annular Contraction and Coaptation

As a soft S1, because the components cancel each other
As a fixed split S1 that widens with inspiration
As a single S1, because a difference under 30 ms is not appreciated

questions.sec: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
questions.q: Which three leaflet abnormalities make S1 soft according to the first factor on page 298?
opts: An incompetent leaky leaflet as in MR, a perforated leaflet as in infective endocarditis, and a calcific immobile leaflet as in calcific MS
An incompetent leaky leaflet as in MR, a perforated leaflet as in rheumatic fever, and a calcific mobile leaflet as in calcific MS
A stenotic leaflet as in MS, a perforated leaflet as in infective endocarditis, and a calcific immobile leaflet as in calcific MS
An incompetent leaky leaflet as in AR, a perforated leaflet as in infective endocarditis, and a calcific immobile leaflet as in calcific AS

questions.sec: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
questions.q: How does the position of the leaflet at end diastole differ in a normal valve and in stenosis, and what does that do to S1?
opts: Normally the leaflet floats wide open in the filled LV, but stenosis reduces LV filling so the valve sits semiclosed and closes from a short distance, making S1 soft
Normally the leaflet floats semiclosed in the filled LV, but stenosis increases LV filling so the valve sits wide apart and closes from a distance, making S1 loud
Normally the leaflet floats semiclosed in the filled LV, but stenosis reduces LV filling so the valve sits wide apart and closes from a distance, making S1 loud
Normally the leaflet floats semiclosed in the empty LV, but stenosis reduces LV filling so the valve sits wide apart and closes from a distance, making S1 loud
questions.exp: The block reads 'Normal: Semiclosed position floating in the filled LV', then stenosis → reduced LV filling → valve wide apart → close from a distance → loud S1, the example being MS. (Book p298)

questions.sec: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
questions.q: Match each heart rate state to its printed effect on S1 — 1) Bradycardia 2) Tachycardia … A) Loud S1 B) Soft S1
questions.exp: Bradycardia lengthens the PR interval, increases filling and brings the valves closer, so S1 is soft; tachycardia shortens the PR interval, reduces filling and makes the valves close from a distance, so S1 is loud. (Book p298)

questions.sec: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
questions.q: Which two timing abnormalities are printed for closure, with their examples?
opts: Delayed closure gives a soft S1 as in MS, and premature closure gives a loud S1 as in AR
Delayed closure gives a loud S1 as in MR, and premature closure gives a soft S1 as in AS
Delayed closure gives a loud S1 as in AR, and premature closure gives a soft S1 as in MS
Delayed closure gives a loud S1 as in MS, and premature closure gives a soft S1 as in AR
questions.exp: The timing block reads 'a. Delayed closure: Loud S1, e.g. MS → ↑LAP → more time for LVP > LAP' and 'b. Premature closure: soft S1, e.g. AR → LVP ↑ rapidly'. (Book p298)

questions.sec: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
questions.q: Which dP/dt states are printed, and which examples accompany them?

A leaky valve preserves dP/dt and gives a loud S1 (MR, myocarditis), while exercise lowers contractility and gives a soft S1
A leaky valve gives loss of dP/dt and a loud S1 (MR, myocarditis), while exercise raises dP/dt and gives a soft S1
A stenotic valve gives loss of dP/dt and a soft S1 (AS, MS), while exercise raises dP/dt and gives a loud S1
questions.exp: The factor reads 'dP/dt of isovolumetric contraction' with a. leaky valve → ineffective IVC → loss of dP/dt → ↓velocity → soft S1 (MR, myocarditis) and b. exercise/high output → ↑contractility → ↑dP/dt → loud S1. (Book p298)

questions.sec: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
questions.q: How do thoracic transmission factors change S1 on page 298?
opts: Obesity, emphysema and pericardial effusion reduce the intensity of S1 alone, while a thin chest wall raises only the murmurs
Obesity, emphysema and pleural effusion reduce the intensity of all auscultatory events giving a soft S1, while a thin chest wall raises intensity
Obesity, emphysema and pericardial effusion reduce the intensity of all auscultatory events giving a soft S1, while a thin chest wall raises intensity giving a loud S1
Obesity, emphysema and pericardial effusion raise the intensity of all auscultatory events giving a loud S1, while a thin chest wall lowers intensity
questions.exp: The sixth factor reads 'Obesity, emphysema, pericardial effusion → ↓intensity of all auscultatory events → soft S1' and 'Thin chest wall → ↑intensity → loud S1'. (Book p298)

questions.sec: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
questions.q: A young woman with a long PR interval on ECG has a strikingly soft first heart sound. Which printed mechanism explains it?
opts: Bradycardia shortens diastole, so filling is less, the valve leaflets sit wide apart and closure velocity rises
Bradycardia lengthens diastole, so filling is greater, the valve leaflets sit closer and closure velocity falls
The long PR interval delays closure, so the leaflets travel further and S1 becomes loud
The long PR interval perforates the leaflets, so S1 becomes soft
questions.exp: The velocity-of-contraction block explicitly ties '↑ PR interval (diastole) → ↑ filling → valve are closer → ↓ velocity' to a soft S1 in bradycardia. (Book p298)

questions.sec: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
questions.q: A patient with calcific mitral stenosis has a soft first heart sound. Which of the six printed factors explains it?
opts: The valve sits wide apart at end diastole and closes from a distance
The chest wall is thin, dampening transmission
Loss of leaflet integrity, because the calcific leaflet is immobile
The PR interval is short, reducing filling before closure

units.title: Heart Sounds as Discrete Vibrations, Intensity in Decibels against Frequency in Hertz with Their Inverse Relation, the Six-Row High against Low Frequency Table and the Mixed ESM of Aortic Stenosis
units.sec: Heart Sounds as Discrete Vibrations, Intensity in Decibels against Frequency in Hertz with Their Inverse Relation, the Six-Row High against Low Frequency Table and the Mixed ESM of Aortic Stenosis
units.guide:
Heart sounds (p296) are brief, discrete auditory vibrations; intensity is measured in decibels and frequency in hertz, with frequency ∝ 1/amplitude.
High frequency sounds are soft, musical or blowing, with a wide chamber pressure difference, a wider area, no thrill and the diaphragm; low frequency sounds are rough, rumbling or thud-like, with a low pressure difference, a localised area, a thrill and the bell, whose exceptions are S3, S4, tumour plop, MS, TS and Austin Flint.
The mixed frequency sound is the ejection systolic murmur of AS — harsh at the 2nd right ICS, with low pitch radiating to the carotid and high pitch to the apex (Gallavardin).

units.title: The 0.8-Second Cycle, the 0.3-Second Systolic and 0.5-Second Diastolic Phase Lists, the 70 to 30 Per Cent Filling Split, and the S1 Valve Apparatus with Annular Contraction and Coaptation
units.sec: The 0.8-Second Cycle, the 0.3-Second Systolic and 0.5-Second Diastolic Phase Lists, the 70 to 30 Per Cent Filling Split, and the S1 Valve Apparatus with Annular Contraction and Coaptation
units.guide:
The cardiac cycle (p297) lasts 0.8 s, atrial systole 0.1 s against atrial diastole 0.7 s; systole 0.3 s holds isovolumetric contraction, rapid ejection and reduced ejection, and diastole 0.5 s holds protodiastole, isovolumetric relaxation, rapid filling, reduced filling and atrial systole.
During reduced filling the AV valves are open and 70% of filling is passive, atrial systole adds 30%, then ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure, the AV valves close and S1 is born into isovolumetric contraction.
The valve apparatus is leaflet, fibrous annulus and commissures; annular contraction → coaptation → sudden tensing gives S1, whose M1 and T1 lie <30 ms apart and are not appreciated separately.

units.title: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
units.sec: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
units.guide:
Six factors alter S1 intensity (p298): leaflet integrity (incompetent MR, perforated endocarditis and calcific MS all soften it); diastolic leaflet position (stenosis keeps the valve wide apart so it closes from a distance and is loud, as in MS); contraction velocity (bradycardia with a long PR softens, tachycardia with a short PR loudens).
Closure timing decides too — delayed closure is loud in MS while premature closure is soft in AR — and dP/dt behaves the same way, a leaky valve losing dP/dt and softening as in MR or myocarditis while exercise and high output louden.
Chest-wall transmission closes the list: obesity, emphysema and pericardial effusion soften all auscultatory events, whereas a thin chest wall loudens them.

units.title: S1 in Aortic Stenosis, Regurgitation, Mitral Stenosis and Mitral Regurgitation, Loud T1 Causes, the Aortic Ejection Click, and Varying, Intermittent and Wide Split S1
units.sec: S1 in Aortic Stenosis, Regurgitation, Mitral Stenosis and Mitral Regurgitation, Loud T1 Causes, the Aortic Ejection Click, and Varying, Intermittent and Wide Split S1
units.guide:
S1 is normal in AS, soft in AR from premature closure, loud and unrelated to severity in MS from wide-apart position, increased velocity and delayed closure, and soft and unrelated to severity in MR from loss of integrity and loss of dP/dt (p299).
Loud T1 comes from TS, ASD and total anomalous pulmonary venous connection through increased tricuspid flow; the loud sound of AS is an aortic ejection click from a bicuspid valve that can be mistaken for S1; rheumatic MR with a preserved leaflet gives a soft S1 from myocarditis, MS with MR depends on the predominant lesion, and TR after pulmonary hypertension in moderate MS softens S1.
Variable S1 varies in atrial fibrillation and flutter but is intermittent as cannon S1 in complete heart block and VT with AV dissociation; wide split S1 separates early M1 (LV ectopic or pacing, Ebstein with a sail sound) from late T1 (RBBB, TS, RA myxoma).

units.title: Reverse Split S1, the S1 to S2 Sequence through Crossover Pressure, and the Hangout Interval with Its 30 and 80 Millisecond Aortic and Pulmonary Values
units.sec: Reverse Split S1, the S1 to S2 Sequence through Crossover Pressure, and the Hangout Interval with Its 30 and 80 Millisecond Aortic and Pulmonary Values
units.guide:
Reverse split of S1 puts T1 before M1, from early T1 in right sided pacing or ectopic and from delayed M1 in LBBB or, mechanically, MS and LA myxoma (p300).
After S1 the aortic and pulmonary valves open with ejection clicks, then rapid and reduced ejection raise aortic and pulmonary pressures to the crossover point, where aortic pressure exceeds CVP and pulmonary pressure exceeds RVP.
The hangout interval runs from crossover pressure to valve closure and depends on pressure beyond the valve and vessel distensibility, printing 30 ms for the aorta and 80 ms for the pulmonary artery; the A2–P2 gap is 50 ms and appreciable, exceeding 50 ms in inspiration from increased venous return.

units.title: S2 as Aortic and Pulmonary Closure at 120–150 Hz, the Four Determinants of A2 and P2, Their Behaviour in Valve Disease, the Four-Column Table and the Six Causes of a Single S2
units.sec: S2 as Aortic and Pulmonary Closure at 120–150 Hz, the Four Determinants of A2 and P2, Their Behaviour in Valve Disease, the Four-Column Table and the Six Causes of a Single S2
units.guide:
S2 is aortic and pulmonary closure at a high frequency of 120–150 Hz, with A2 louder because aortic pressure exceeds pulmonary pressure (p301).
A2 and P2 are governed by pressure beyond the valve (systemic HTN loudens A2, pulmonary HTN loudens P2), flow across the valve (hyperkinetic states louden both), valve mobility and vessel dilatation beyond the valve.
AS from a bicuspid valve is loud but degenerative AS is soft, AR is soft from valve pathology and loud (tambour S2) from root disease such as syphilis, moderate MS loudens P2 and with RVF widens the split, and MR loudens P2 only with pulmonary hypertension; single S2 arises in severe PAH (single loud P2), aging, semilunar atresia, severe AS or PS and truncus arteriosus.

units.title: Wide Split S2 above 50 ms with Its Variable and Fixed Arms, and the Paradoxical Split with Early P2 and Delayed A2 Causes
units.sec: Wide Split S2 above 50 ms with Its Variable and Fixed Arms, and the Paradoxical Split with Early P2 and Delayed A2 Causes
units.guide:
A wide split of S2 exceeds 50 ms and is heard even in expiration (p302).
Its variable causes are early A2 (LV pacing or ectopic electrically, MR mechanically) and late P2 (RBBB, pulmonary hypertension with RVF as in MS, PS, VSD with a left-to-right shunt, cardiac tamponade).
Fixed splitting is any wide variable split with significant RV failure, or ASD where RV and LV filling change equally with respiration; the reverse or paradoxical split is heard in expiration with P2 before A2, from early P2 (right sided pacing/ectopic, WPW type B, TR) or delayed A2 (LBBB, AS, AR, HCM).
